findings.title: Providers with equal order() are picked by classpath order, silently
findings.body: detectProvider no longer rejects multiple providers. It stable-sorts by order() and takes the first entry. DefaultCryptoProvider (line 84), WildFlyElytronProvider (line 77) and FIPS1402Provider (line 115) all return 200. When two of them are on the same classpath, the winner is whichever ServiceLoader discovered first. Before this PR that case threw IllegalStateException; now it only logs at debug level. In a FIPS deployment that also has the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider on the classpath, the non-FIPS provider can be chosen with no error. Ties need a deterministic rule (for example, FIPS ranked above default) or should still fail. No test covers this selection logic.

findings.title: Non-selected providers are constructed, and their constructors mutate global JVM security state
findings.body: The ServiceLoader stream is collected into a list before sorting, so every discovered CryptoProvider constructor runs, including those that will not be selected. FIPS1402Provider's constructor (FIPS1402Provider.java line 94) inserts a KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider at JVM security slot 1. When BCFIPS is absent it also inserts BCFIPS and BCJSSE and rewrites the ssl.KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory properties. DefaultCryptoProvider's constructor registers a non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider with Security.addProvider. Previously these side effects were followed by a hard failure when more than one provider was present. Now the multi-provider case succeeds, so the side effects persist in a JVM that runs a different provider. Discovery should avoid constructing unselected providers, for example by ranking on metadata before instantiation.

findings.title: AuthzClient.create() can pin the process-wide crypto provider to the minimal one
findings.body: CryptoIntegration.init is process-global and effectively runs once, using the class loader of AuthzClient. If that loader cannot see the full crypto provider (for example, when the real crypto jar is in another class loader, such as an application server module), or if an application creates an AuthzClient before anything else initializes crypto, the global provider becomes AuthzClientCryptoProvider. Because init is a no-op afterwards, later code that needs the real provider keeps getting AuthzClientCryptoProvider, and most of its methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. Before this change AuthzClient did not touch the global provider. Consider not installing a placeholder provider globally from this entry point.

findings.title: Most provider methods throw a 'Not supported yet.' placeholder
findings.body: About 17 methods, including getAlgorithmProvider, getCertificateUtils, getPemUtils, getKeyFactory, getSignature, getSecretKeyFact, getX509CertFactory and wrapFactoryForTruststore, throw UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.'). That is leftover IDE template text, and it suggests the feature is planned. Because this provider is now a global ServiceLoader entry, callers that reach it through CryptoIntegration.getProvider() get an opaque failure. The message should say the provider is limited to ECDSA conversion, or the methods should be implemented.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK keystore provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: The method builds a new, uninitialized KeyStore of the default type and returns its Provider, which is normally the JDK's SUN provider. Callers of getBouncyCastleProvider() that expect BouncyCastle, for example to look up algorithms by provider name, get the JDK provider silently. The method also allocates a throwaway KeyStore on every call. It should either return a real BC provider or throw UnsupportedOperationException like the other unimplemented methods.

findings.title: concatenatedRSToASN1DER does not validate signature length
findings.body: The method copies signature[len..2*len) without checking signature.length. A short or malformed signature triggers an unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException rather than an IOException or a clean verification failure. The method is copied from the BC implementation but is new code here, so it should check that signature.length equals signLength.

findings.title: Dead ASN1Encoder calls whose results are discarded
findings.body: Lines 114 and 115 create ASN1Encoder instances and discard the result. The returned DER sequence on lines 117-121 recomputes the same encodings. The dead calls look like a leftover and make the method harder to read.

findings.title: New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: order() is added to the public CryptoProvider interface without a default implementation. Any existing implementation that does not override it, including out-of-tree providers, is not broken at compile time but throws AbstractMethodError. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider calls order() on every discovered provider, so such a provider fails during crypto initialization. A default method, for example returning 0, would keep existing implementations working.

findings.title: Test only checks the module's own encoder and decoder round-trip
findings.body: The assertion compares the concatenated R||S produced by asn1derToConcatenatedRS with the value obtained after encoding and decoding it again, using the same class. If both directions share a defect, or if the produced DER is not accepted by a standard verifier, the test still passes. The test should verify the DER output from concatenatedRSToASN1DER with java.security.Signature.verify, or check it against a known test vector.

findings.title: ES384 and ES512 are tested with a P-256 key, so the real component sizes are not exercised
findings.body: A single default EC key pair is used for ES256, ES384 and ES512, so ES384 and ES512 sign with P-256 keys. The 48-byte and 66-byte component paths are not tested with matching curves. The P-521 case matters most: R can be 66 bytes plus a sign byte, which hits the truncation branch in integerToBytes, and that path is never exercised. The test therefore gives false confidence for ES384 and ES512. Each algorithm should be tested with its own curve, P-384 and P-521.
